in writing. - i support the podimata report on innovative finance with reservations. i share the rapporteur's concern about the economic and financial crisis we are going through and its consequences for the lack of investment. i also agree that it is desirable that investment should translate into more progress and innovation and that europe needs to increase its capacity for smart investment. i am afraid that, as a whole, the report seems excessively inclined towards raising taxes and charges when in different countries (such as portugal) we are already seeing an overdose of tax burdens. the final version of the report ends by encouraging the introduction of a financial transaction tax (at global or at least european level), while admitting that it is necessary to study its consequences (for which i am planning an ex post study). i welcome the defence of the launch of eurobonds, which would facilitate market access for the weaker euro countries, and the view that this would be beneficial 'for all participating member states and for the euro area as a whole'.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report for advocating the creation of specific instruments, such as the introduction of a financial transaction tax, which can help to improve market efficiency, increase transparency, reduce excessive price volatility and create incentives for the financial sector to make long-term investments with added value for the real economy.
in writing. − this report focuses on the need to find new ways of financing the public sector at global and european level. in fact, the current economic and financial crisis has forced member states to look for revenue to mitigate budgetary crises. among the new means of financing are taxation of the financial sector and co2 emissions. in recent times, the financial sector has been distorting its objectives of financing the economy in order to develop it, but, under the pretext of needing to cover risks, it raises rates and immediately obtains huge profits that seriously affect public finances and citizens. on the other hand, a tax on co2 emissions will make the polluter-pays principle fairer and more consistent, contributing not only to reducing climate change but also to financing investment projects in this area. i agree with the idea of a global financial transaction tax. i believe that its introduction at european level should be preceded by an impact study. i also support the introduction of eurobonds as a common debt management instrument.
in writing. - this report is about innovative financing. but it doesn't really come out of the old, stale positions of refusing the most elementary justice. the financial market should have been effectively controlled and regulated long ago. speculation should have been curbed long ago - whether it was on commodities, including food, real estate, pensions and pensions, or sovereign debts of states (just to name a few). but the european commission is adamant that it will not go ahead with these proposals. even though the financial damage caused by tax evasion and fraud in europe is estimated at between 200 and 250 billion euros a year, enough to reduce public deficits without having to raise taxes on labour - the old solution. the commission is also adamant that it will not introduce a financial transaction tax at eu level and that it will not push for its adoption at world level. the same applies to the scandalous persistence of tax havens. they would be ways to raise revenue to fight poverty and other persistent economic and social problems. current estimates of revenue generation from a financial transaction tax, even at the reduced rate, indicate that it would generate around eur 200 billion per year at eu level.
in writing. - effective control and regulation of the capital market has long been required, preventing speculation on a wide range of products, from raw materials to real estate transactions, pensions, pensions and insurance, with a whole range of derivative products, including sovereign debt itself. unfortunately, the european commission has not moved forward with these proposals when it is known that the financial damage caused by tax evasion and fraud in europe is estimated at between 200 and 250 billion euros per year, which alone would be enough to reduce public deficits without the need to increase taxes on labour. but if we also had taxes on financial transactions at world level and therefore also in the european union, in addition to the end of tax havens and speculative financial products, we would still have superior values to deal with economic and social problems. current estimates of revenue generation from a financial transaction tax, even at the reduced rate, indicate that it would generate around eur 200 billion per year at the level of the european union. in this context, we cannot accept that a clear position on the creation of a financial transaction tax be postponed on the pretext of further studies and new assessments.
in writing. - while i agree with much of the content of this report, i could not vote for it after the introduction of a financial transaction tax (global or at least european) but i do accept that its consequences need to be studied (for which i am planning an a posteriori study). the party i represent has always fought in portugal against the introduction of this financial transaction tax, because of the harmful effect it could have on the financial markets. portugal is exhausted and unable to cope with the additional tax burden, since this tax would ultimately be borne by the citizens, as the financial institutions would reflect it on the customers. the introduction of such a tax at european level alone may lead to other markets having competitive advantages over european financial markets.
in writing. − this report is about innovative financing measures at global and european level. this is to outline measures to address the serious weaknesses in the regulatory and supervisory framework of the global financial system that were revealed by the global economic and financial crisis of 2007-2009. financial transactions are characterised today by a huge increase in volume and a marked discrepancy between the volume of financial transactions and the needs associated with them in the real world. new trading models, such as short-term investing and automated high-frequency trading, which have taken a central role in global financial trends and have led to excessive volatility and risk-taking, deserve the attention of policymakers. these are sufficient reasons for the european parliament, within the framework of its powers, to make its contribution and indicate the measures it considers appropriate to resolve the situation.
in writing. − in order to cope with the global financial crisis and the ensuing deep recession, several governments have increased sovereign debt to unsustainable levels in order to bail out financial firms and stimulate their economies. at the same time, banks accumulate profits through the difference between the loans they obtain from the central bank at a near-zero interest rate and the price at which they grant credit to their customers and to the states. it is therefore a moral imperative that the financial business take responsibility for the crisis it has caused. a financial transaction tax is the minimum required. to those who wish to postpone this responsibility, on the pretext that such a tax can only be introduced on a global scale, i say: (1) that the eu's position would be strongly strengthened by the unilateral launch of the said tax; (2) if some of the capital invested in speculative transactions were to leave the eu, this would result in a reduction in financial market volatility, which is beneficial; (3) if overall financial regulation is neither feasible nor prudent, sensible rules on capital movements are needed. the report goes in that direction.
in writing. − the economic and financial crisis has revealed the serious weaknesses in the regulatory and supervisory framework of the global financial system. new instruments are needed to respond to the crisis, which can stop speculation and restore the role of the financial sector, ensure fair burden sharing and create new additional resources to address global challenges such as climate change, the development goals and smart, sustainable and inclusive growth under the eu2020 strategy. this own-initiative report is intended to find new and innovative sources of funding. the revenue-based taxation instruments are considered to be insufficient. the document explores the following innovative financing possibilities: taxation of the financial sector, eurobonds and taxation of the energy sector. in my view, it is essential to innovate in terms of alternative means of financing that are up to the challenges of today and in line with the world today, but it is unwise to do so without first studying their actual impact. as important as increasing revenues is the need to step up the regulatory role of the market by creating mechanisms that can enhance its transparency, efficiency and stability. for these reasons i voted in favour of the document in plenary.
in writing. - i am voting in favour of this report because the importance of reducing health inequalities is intrinsically linked to the reduction of social inequalities, as this report points out. health inequalities start at an early age and continue throughout life, as they are also reproduced in other generations. in this sense, the member states have a duty to adopt the health principle in all their policies. i also strongly support the rapporteur's recommendations that universal access to health care, including for undocumented migrants, and access to social protection for pregnant women, in accordance with the legislation in their countries, should be promoted.
in writing. − european citizens are now living longer and healthier lives. although average levels of health in the european union have improved over time, health disparities between and within member states still exist in europe, and these disparities are likely to increase due to the current economic, financial and social crisis. as the shadow rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, i pointed out the need to find solutions. these will necessarily involve all the actors: the european union, national governments, regional and local authorities and the social economy. the challenges facing the european union as a result of demographic change call for a concrete plan to tackle health inequalities in rural areas. strengthening the mechanism for the recognition of qualifications will facilitate the circulation of skills in the eu and the mobility of professionals. campaigns on the promotion of healthy lifestyles and prevention and screening programmes targeted at specific groups are also important in reducing health inequalities. i therefore support this report.
in writing. - i share the view of rapporteur edite estrela that there are huge disparities in health, both between people living in different regions of the eu and between the more and less privileged groups of the population. these inequalities tend to start at birth and eventually persist into old age, influenced throughout life by access to education, employment, health care, and can be exacerbated by differences based on gender and race. reducing the size of existing disparities, which call into question the eu's commitments to solidarity, social and economic cohesion, human rights and equal opportunities, is essential and therefore one of the priority actions of the eu health strategy 2008-2013. it should, however, be recognised that health policy is a matter for the member states and that they have the responsibility for defining their systems for providing access to health care. the report provides for a number of interesting measures but avoids equating their financial impact. i also regret the introduction of the question of abortion, which is a matter for national rather than european competence.
in writing. − although the report contains provisions which i consider to be of the greatest relevance on the growing importance of health care for the elderly and the need to develop a deeper understanding of the pathologies which affect the elderly in particular, it generically brings little new information. in fact, by wanting to talk about everything, it ends up becoming a 'catalogue of intentions' in which the rapporteur, under the pretext of 'reducing inequalities in health', brings together such diverse subjects - and unrelated to equal access to health - as domestic violence, the pharmaceutical sector inquiry, the policies of the states with regard to voluntary termination of pregnancy and access to fertility treatment for homosexuals. i do not think that is the context in which they should be dealt with. we know that access to abortion and assisted reproduction for homosexual couples is a controversial issue in the states and only they should be able to decide freely on them. for this reason too, i cannot vote in favour of the report.
in writing. − health and life expectancy are closely linked to social conditions. it is essential that reducing inequalities is considered a key priority at all levels of policy action, thus pursuing the health strategy in all policies and ensuring effective impact assessments. indeed, inequalities persist, as evidenced by the fact that life expectancy at birth in 2007 varied by 14.2 years for men and 8.3 years for women between member states. universal access to health systems and affordable health care for all needs to be improved. it is important to improve access to disease prevention, health promotion, as well as to primary and specialised health services, and to reduce inequalities between different social groups. however, i did not vote in favour of the report because i do not agree with paragraph 29 and i quote urges the eu and the member states to take the necessary measures in terms of access to assisted reproductive technologies (art) in order to eliminate discrimination against women on grounds of marital status, age, sexual orientation or ethnic or cultural origin.
in writing. - the report contains a set of guidelines which we consider valid and fair. we cannot, however, fail to make some repairs. the so-called austerity policies, which are profoundly anti-social in their essence and content, with cuts in public investment, in the social functions of the state - particularly in health - among other extremely damaging consequences from an economic and social point of view, are also increasing inequalities in the area of health. when, in the name of the need to reduce the budget deficit, rates of access to public health services are increased, medicines are increased, even for chronic diseases, by reducing public co-financing, support for the transport of patients for treatment and health consultations is eliminated where there is no public transport, health inequalities are being aggravated, as is currently the case in portugal. in fact, people with lower incomes have increasingly difficulty in accessing health care. more than mere words, what is needed is a real change in the content of policies. we must put an end to neoliberal policies and ensure effective equality of opportunity, including in access to health care.
in writing. - this report addresses a number of important issues, but does not go into the depths of the problems that are currently being caused by austerity policies and anti-social policies that increase health inequalities. so, words are not enough! the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of health care in the member states. the stability pact must be abolished to prevent the need to reduce the budget deficit from increasing access to public health services, increasing medicines, even for chronic diseases, and eliminating support for the transport of patients for treatment and health consultations, even in areas where there is no public transport. we know that the result of these policies is the increase in health inequalities, as is happening right now in portugal. people on lower incomes have increasingly difficulty in accessing health care. so more than just fine words, we need a break and a change of policies to give priority to respect for human rights and economic and social cohesion.
in writing. − this report highlights health inequalities between eu citizens, men and women, young and old, which are linked to a wide range of factors: economic, social, educational, occupational contexts, living conditions. it emphasises the importance of maintaining and improving universality and access to high-quality healthcare for all, including, among other vulnerable groups, undocumented immigrants. it points out that the economic and financial crisis and the austerity measures imposed by the member states have had a serious impact on the health sector and that this will lead to further inequalities. the report calls on the commission and the member states to develop a common set of indicators to monitor health inequalities and to pursue the 'health in all policies' strategy. it also stresses the importance of preventive action and a 'local care approach'. in view of the above and in order to encourage the suggestions contained in the report, i voted in favour.
in writing. the report we have voted on deals with some important issues, particularly as regards the defence of equal health care for all, which unfortunately is not yet the case in the eu, particularly among the most disadvantaged populations such as children, the elderly and women in some cases. however, and in my opinion, many other subjects are dealt with that have nothing to do with health. however, what shocks me most is the way in which the policies of the states are approached with regard to voluntary termination of pregnancy and access to fertility treatment for homosexuals, which in my view should respect the principle of subsidiarity and be treated in a less discriminatory way. that is why i am voting against this report.
in writing. − this report on reducing health inequalities in the eu presents a number of measures which i consider to be worthwhile and important. however, i abstained in the final vote on the report because i could not agree with the duty of the eu and the member states to guarantee women full free access to abortion. the investment must always be made in family planning and contraception, with abortion being a last resort for exceptional situations. i also do not believe that assisted reproductive technologies (art) should be open access, but should be subordinated to the principle of subsidiarity and should never be used as a tool for eliminating discrimination against women on grounds of marital status, age, sexual orientation or ethnic or cultural origin.
in writing. the report also calls for the establishment of a european network of national experts in the field of health and safety at work. we have a duty to transfer our experience of economic governance so that developing countries can establish their own tax systems. only in this way will it be possible to create a fairer, more equitable and sustainable tax system, to combat tax evasion and, consequently, to promote a better international tax environment. i would also like to stress the importance of this report in calling attention to the urgency of ending tax havens, a key measure in the area of transparency which will allow for the necessary automatic exchange of information in the tax field.
in writing. - the increasing globalisation of markets and the movement of taxpayers has made taxation a complicated issue today. the situation in developing countries is more complex and difficult to correct, due to internal factors such as the large informal sectors, the predominance of agriculture and the limited use of new technologies. i welcome the commission's initiative to cooperate with these countries to promote good governance in tax matters, through a report identifying the main problems and solutions, in order to promote synergies between tax policy and development policy, making both more efficient.
in writing. − the existence of efficient, transparent and equitable tax systems is crucial for the development of the developing countries as it contributes to the financing of their public assets, the sustainability of their institutions, the reduction of dependence on external aid and the achievement of the millennium development goals. in this context, i believe that the eu should, on the one hand, focus on the fight against tax havens and tax evasion (which weaken the political and economic system in developing countries by encouraging economic crime and inequality in the redistribution of tax revenues) and, on the other hand, establish a process of cooperation and dialogue with the tax administrations of these countries. i would also like to stress the importance of widening the tax base in these countries. it should be noted that the tax systems of developing countries are characterised by a system based on indirect taxation (where most of the revenue is derived from the taxation of goods and services), which constrains the collection of tax revenue and results in the inefficiency of these systems. efforts should be concentrated on the development of direct taxation. the need to promote coherence between development policy and the european union's trade policy is equally important.
in writing. − this report is based on a commission document which recognises the link between the achievement of the millennium development goals and good fiscal governance. the report aims to promote greater synergies between fiscal policy and development policy, making both more efficient, and identifies the difficulties in developing countries in mobilising tax revenue. the report also proposes ways for the union to improve the use of existing funds and instruments. stresses the importance of supporting effective and sustainable tax systems, including by combating tax fraud and evasion, in order to contribute to a transparent and fair international tax environment, including in helping to combat tax havens. indeed, it is through good economic governance that these countries will be able to replace dependence on external aid, contributing to the development of the public and private sectors and economic growth.
in writing. - this report deals with taxation and development in developing countries. to achieve the objectives set by the un in 2000 in the millennium declaration, these countries must be able to promote good governance in tax matters, maximising all external support. the european commission, interested in cooperation with these countries, published in 2009 the document taxation and development cooperation with developing countries to promote good governance in tax matters, aiming to promote synergies between development policy and tax policy in order to make them fairer, more transparent and more effective. the same resolution was adopted by the ep in 2010. the eu is aware that fairer and more coherent tax systems will help reduce poverty and compensate for some lost revenue. i therefore support this report which calls for an end to tax havens - the real weapons of destruction for developing countries - fights economic crime, prevents tax evasion and unfair competition, and promotes development through good governance.
in writing. the report identifies a number of relevant and topical issues, including: - making the fight against tax havens and corruption a top priority; - the difficulties faced by developing countries in collecting revenue at home, given that multiple exemptions are granted to large domestic and foreign companies to attract investment; - the tax on international financial transactions, with 'an eu-wide first step'; - low-income countries need the capacity to negotiate efficiently with multinational companies in order to impose capital controls and to be able to exercise their full sovereignty. this report is not without contradictions, however, particularly when, in identifying the problems which will arise from the application of the epas, particularly as regards the reduction of tax revenue, it does not take a clear position in rejecting them. it has no substantive position on the responsibilities of the world bank, the imf and the wto in promoting policies which promote the destruction of the productive machinery and public services, create unemployment and weaken the internal markets of these countries, thus further weakening their tax revenues, their budgets, their sovereignty and independence.
in writing. - while recognising that cooperation in the field of taxation can be important, it must not be overlooked that tax policy is a fundamental instrument of economic and social policy, in the definition of which obvious political criteria and assessments are important. it is not therefore the european union's job to export what is known as good governance in the tax field. the sovereignty of developing countries, their choices and options, taking into account their specific situation and conditions, must be fully respected. however, the so-called economic partnership agreements, which have been imposed on developing countries despite their resistance, in addition to other serious disadvantages, place a very heavy burden on their tax systems by the significant reduction in customs revenue that they imply. on the other hand, tax havens, which are still there, lead to the loss of very high revenues for developing countries every year. the european union must therefore change its policies and resolve these contradictions.
in writing. - it is a fact that poor fiscal governance is detrimental to the good economic performance of member states. the commission now recognises the link between the achievement of the millennium development goals and good fiscal governance. it is therefore imperative to combat tax evasion and to take concrete steps to harmonise these measures across the eu, as it is known that some countries are more effective than others in combating tax fraud and evasion.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report on taxation and development cooperation with developing countries to promote good governance in tax matters, as i consider it, as does the rapporteur, to be important for the development of an efficient tax system in developing countries. the tax system must become the central structure of public finances in developing countries. the new eu investment policy in developing countries should contribute to the establishment of a more favourable environment for domestic and foreign private investment and to the creation of conditions for more effective international assistance. in fact, to promote growth, eu investment policy should focus on the development of smes, including microcredit, the efficiency of public services, public-private partnerships and knowledge transfer. the european commission working paper published in april 2009 entitled 'taxation and development cooperation with developing countries to promote good governance in tax matters' provides guidance and methodologies for promoting synergies between tax policy and development policy to make both more efficient.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this report because it clearly recognises the link between the achievement of the mdgs and fiscal governance, that taxation through a progressive tax regime is essential for democracy, that offshore centres and tax havens target illicit capital flight which, combined with zero tax regimes to attract funds and investment, result in a transfer of burdens to lower income workers and families by reducing the quality and quantity of public services in poor countries as well as their ability to combat poverty. assisting the judicial and anti-corruption authorities and services of developing countries in their efforts to develop progressive tax systems would be an excellent service provided by the eu.
in writing. - i welcome this report, stressing the importance of the recommendations of the papastamkos report, which recalls that non-trade aspects (ntas) should be better incorporated into the wto negotiations. the need for some coherence between the cap and the eu's external trade policy is clear, it is essential to ensure a level playing field for eu producers on the world market, which should not promote unfair competition. if this is not negotiated, european farmers will continue to face unfair competition and will suffer losses and discrimination vis-à-vis competitors outside the european union.
in writing. - i agree with the need for greater coherence between the cap and external trade policy in order to ensure the european agricultural model and, therefore, the equal conditions of european producers vis-à-vis the world market. it is essential to reconcile commercial and non-commercial concerns and to achieve the necessary regulatory convergence.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report on 'agriculture and international trade' because it stresses the importance of integrating non-trade aspects into the development of the doha agenda, such as social, environmental, human health and animal health and welfare considerations, in order to achieve the highest environmental and social standards and to avoid a decline in the competitiveness of eu farmers in the context of world agricultural production.
in writing. - agriculture has social functions which go beyond the mere limits of food production, such as the settlement and planning of the territory, the protection of the environment and the preservation of the cultural traditions of the peoples. i believe that they are very much deserving of protection and follow-up by the member states and the european institutions. despite my principled position in favour of greater market opening, i believe that in the agricultural sector particular rigour must be shown in the requirements of reciprocity and the need to ensure food safety for european consumers. the european union must bear in mind the need to balance the conflicting values and, especially in the current economic and financial crisis, take account of the impact of the trade agreements it concludes on the lives of european farmers and their holdings.
in writing. - one of the sectors most affected by the free movement of persons and goods was agriculture. despite the constant changes to the common agricultural policy (cap) - seen as a symbol of european integration - the sector remains in a highly precarious situation, having to comply with stringent standards of environmental protection and product safety - aggravated by the current financial crisis. this is a sector which is intersecting with other areas such as trade, the environment, industry, transport, etc., which make it very difficult to adopt a regulatory framework which satisfies all the parties involved. despite progress such as the sps (sanitary and phytosanitary measures) and tbt (technical barriers to trade) agreements, much remains to be done. i endorse this report because it recognises the key role of the agri-food sector within the eu and that it is a very sensitive sector which cannot face aggressive competition - which will have to be taken into account when new agreements are signed. i hope, however, that the new economic framework of the cap will improve the coordination between productivity and the international market.
in writing. - this is a report full of contradictions. it points to the negative consequences of trade liberalisation, but does not oppose the course of policies which are at the root of the main problems of agriculture in eu countries (and also in developing countries). nothing is proposed to change that course. it rightly criticises the commission's approach which puts agricultural interests behind the interests of industry and the service sector, which makes concessions on agriculture in order to gain greater market access in third countries. he gives examples of the disastrous consequences of this policy - the case of sugar is paradigmatic. it recognises that greater liberalisation of world trade in agricultural products, enhanced by wto agreements, has so far not been able to sustain the threat of hunger in the world. but it does not condemn or oppose this trend towards deeper liberalization and deregulation of world trade, which the eu has been promoting, whether in the framework of the wto or in the framework of numerous bilateral agreements. on the contrary, defend him. the criticism and denunciation of the failure of neoliberal policies has been going on for a long time. the report does so, albeit in a very nuanced and sometimes ambiguous way. then they come back to bail out the disaster policy. we consider it unacceptable.
in writing. - we already know many examples of the disastrous consequences of the liberalization of world trade in the agricultural sector. but this report draws attention to several cases, not hiding that agriculture has been used as a bargaining chip in favour of other interests in the wto negotiations, in particular the interests of the large service groups and international trade and some high-tech industries. we therefore advocate other solutions, since the report was not consistent. we want international trade to be guided by a logic of complementarity and not of competition - between countries, producers and products. we want an agriculture geared to safeguarding the food sovereignty and security of each country, which counters the dangerous anarchy of production towards a liberalised market.
in writing. - this report underlines that the eu has a duty to contribute to world food security, and i congratulate it on this. however, despite mentioning several of the harmful consequences of market liberalisation in agriculture, the solutions they point to are again in the direction of strengthening free trade, subordinating agricultural policies to the interests of the wto. the report explicitly threatens argentina for not complying with the wto by restricting imports of food products that compete with domestic production. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'common carrier' to cover all transport services. the situation in brazil is not precisely described. i therefore voted against this report, since it gives priority to liberalization and competition on agricultural markets.
in writing. - agricultural products are an essential part of international trade and should therefore be recognised as such. there is no doubt, therefore, that the steady rise in food prices, as a consequence of increases in raw materials, is an increasingly pressing concern of the eu. on the other hand, the agricultural sector has to meet the food needs of an increasing number of people, despite facing increasingly limited natural resources and high prices of production factors, as well as environmental and resource conservation concerns, especially in developed economies, which can lead to distortions of competition. in view of future needs, there is no doubt that agriculture must become a strategic sector, i would even say a crucial one, for the economic development of the eu and the world.
in writing. - i voted against the european parliament resolution on 'agriculture and international trade' because i believe that it subordinates the union's trade policy entirely to agricultural policy, when it is well known that only trade policy can guarantee access to external markets for our industry, our services and even our agriculture, access which is essential for economic growth and job creation in the union. if the political orientation of this resolution is followed in future, it will be virtually impossible to conclude trade agreements with countries or regions with an agricultural dimension, such as brazil or india. the common commercial policy - which concerns the whole of the union and all the member states - cannot be completely hostage to the interests of the agricultural sector, which, moreover, concerns a limited number of member states. i also regret that this resolution, in the case of brazil, contains completely unfounded accusations, as has been amply demonstrated by the brazilian side.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because it clearly defends the interests of european farmers in the context of international trade. i believe that external trade policy should not undermine the eu's ability to maintain a strong agricultural sector and to ensure food security in a context of increased market volatility. the commission, however, often gives in to the interests of agriculture in order to achieve greater market access in third countries for industrial products and services. in addition, it should be borne in mind that the european agricultural sector is obliged to respect the highest standards in terms of quality, product hygiene, sustainable production methods, plant and animal health and welfare, traceability, pesticide residue control, veterinary medicine and additives - all of which are cost-intensive aspects of production and which should be taken into account in multilateral and bilateral negotiations. in general terms, i believe that decisions should not be taken to open up the community market to imports of agricultural products without first carrying out impact studies and ensuring that eu farmers are compensated for their losses.
in writing. − the balance between the common agricultural, development and trade policies is fundamental for the european union. the european agricultural sector deserves particular attention. the cap is the oldest community policy and must remain strong. i would like to remind you of the multifunctional role of this sector and its necessary link with other social and political objectives, such as the eu2020 objectives. european agriculture is not, however, isolated from european external relations, particularly in the fields of international trade and development aid. the importance of international relations, particularly through agreements such as the eu and mercosur, is reflected at the economic, political and strategic partnership levels. it is therefore essential to promote regulatory coherence, particularly in the field of agricultural issues. that is why i voted against paragraphs 53 and 54 of the document. in addition, their free trade agreements expose the sector to new challenges and different realities. i would mention the situation of the outermost regions, which have a fragile economy based mainly on agriculture, with production similar to that of their latin american partners. as a member of the european parliament from an outermost region, i would stress the importance of taking account of the specific features of these regions and of trying to avoid compromising their development in the course of future negotiations.
in writing. - i approve this report as i agree that the commission needs to include in the cap reform appropriate and precise measures on instruments which support farmers by improving crop rotation. reducing the protein deficit in the eu must be an essential element in reforming the cap for the benefit of european farmers and the internal market. such measures are extremely useful in view of the fact that protein crops in the eu currently occupy only 3% of arable land and the fact that the eu imports 40 million tonnes of protein crops, which represent 80% of its internal consumption.
in writing. − in view of the decline in protein production in the eu over the last 10 years, there is an urgent need to combat the risk of dependence on international markets and their price volatility. i therefore support the reforms in the cap to introduce new provisions which, in addition to supporting farmers in improving crop rotation systems, promote services and scientific research to support the harvesting of proteaginous seeds. i would also like to mention the importance of a decentralised approach to research programmes which takes account of local farmers' knowledge and sustainable farming systems. i therefore support the proposal to the commission to consider the re-establishment of an agricultural research unit in the directorate-general for agriculture and rural development.
in writing. - according to data in this report, the production of protein crops in the european union has decreased by 30% over the last ten years. the rapporteur adds that 'in the eu, total protein crop production currently occupies only 3% of arable land. despite public support, production of dried legumes declined again to about one million hectares in 2008. more than 40 million tonnes of protein crops are imported annually, representing 80% of protein crop consumption in the eu. "these numbers should be enough to get the attention of political leaders and justify a change in policy. at a time when food prices are reaching historic highs, putting food security at risk, the european union, which is reviewing the cap, cannot but look at the problem of protein crops and try to find a solution. this must necessarily involve greater investment in this crop, which, in addition to reducing imports, improves agriculture's contribution to environmental protection, since protein crops can substantially reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
in writing. - according to recent data released by the european commission, the production of high-protein crops in the european union has suffered a huge decline of around 30%, which shows that something has gone wrong with the common agricultural policy (cap). this situation forces the eu to import more than 40 million tonnes of protein crops and is due to commitments from the past, such as the general agreement on tariffs and trade (gatt) and the blair house agreement, which allowed the import of oilseeds and protein crops free of customs duties. recent climate change has put this issue on the agenda and made it an important element in the cap reform that is expected soon. the cultivation of protein crops, combined with a large rotation of other crops, brings great benefits, not only in environmental terms, but also in terms of cost reduction, as it enriches the soils with respect to nitrogen. i am voting in favour of this report, which aims to reduce the protein deficit in the eu, and i hope that its recommendations, such as support for farmers who want to switch to protein crops and crop rotation, will be taken into account in the preparation of the new cap.
in writing. − the protein deficit in europe and the imbalance between animal and vegetable protein production is a growing problem, with effects on changing human consumption habits, food quality and safety and the crisis facing livestock farmers. the rapporteur is coming up with figures which are illuminating and worrying. numbers that require attention to the problem and specific measures to solve it. these imbalances are rooted in the existing agricultural and trade policies and will not be resolved without a fundamental change in both - a fact which the report omits. the overcoming of the current deficits and imbalances must be based on support for the increase and diversification of protein crops and a policy of progressive import substitution. the report recognises this need and points to some important measures, which we value, such as the creation of market conditions favourable to local production, marketing and consumption and the promotion of short supply chains free of gmos. but at the same time it opens the door to solutions which we regard with concern and which we cannot accept, such as the lifting of the zero tolerance for the presence of gmos in imported animal feed, putting into question the strict application of the precautionary principle.
in writing. - this report seeks to respond to the problem of the protein deficit in europe and the imbalance between animal and vegetable protein production, which, as we know, is a growing problem with effects on changing human consumption habits, food quality and safety and the crisis facing livestock farmers. the imbalances are rooted in the existing agricultural and trade policies and will not be resolved without a fundamental change in both, which the report unfortunately omits. we believe that the overcoming of the present deficits and imbalances must be based on support for the increase and diversification of protein crops and a policy of gradual import substitution. while the report acknowledges this need and points to some important measures, which we appreciate, it nevertheless opens the door to solutions which we regard with concern and which we cannot accept, such as the lifting of the zero tolerance for the presence of gmos in imported animal feed, calling into question the strict application of the precautionary principle.
in writing. − it is essential to increase the production of protein-rich plants in order to reduce dependence on imported soya, maintain food security and benefit the environment. scientific studies are available demonstrating the environmental benefits of protein crops in terms of greenhouse gas emissions, as well as improvement of biodiversity and soil quality. it is very worrying that only 3% of european agricultural production is protein crops. it is not acceptable that we import 80% of our needs. it is therefore very important that in the next support framework, the cap post 2013, measures are taken to change this situation.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the hausling report (a7-0026/2011), as it advocates a supply of protein for animal feed in the eu, a problem which over the years has contributed to a lack of competitiveness of european agriculture. over the last ten years the production of protein crops has been showing a worrying deficit and the situation is currently declining considerably in the european union. the main dry legumes showed a decrease of 30% on average; in the case of soya beans, the value is 12%. this trend exacerbates the union's already alarming dependence on imports of protein crops, mainly used in animal feed, and poses major risks, in particular for the eu livestock sector, a problem exacerbated by price volatility on international markets. it is a priority for the commission to ensure, as a matter of urgency, an unhindered supply of soya beans by presenting a technical solution concerning the low level of gmos in protein crops for food and feed imported into the eu. insufficient imports of soya impose additional costs on the eu livestock and feed sectors and undermine the economic viability of domestic meat production.
in writing. − i approve this 2010 annual report on gender equality in the eu and the recommendations it makes. the current crisis has had a devastating effect on women, although male-dominated occupational sectors have been hit the hardest. i would also point out that there is still a gender pay gap of 18% in the eu, despite the fact that there are more women than men in the workforce. as the main measures that need to be taken, i would stress the development of equality plans and the fight against domestic violence, with the establishment of a european year devoted to this subject.
in writing. − equality between men and women is one of the fundamental principles of community law. the objectives of the european union are to ensure equal opportunities and equal treatment for men and women and to combat all discrimination based on sex. despite all the efforts made in the european union to achieve equality between men and women, inequalities still exist in this area. the employment rate for women (58.6%) remains lower than for men (70.7%), despite the fact that the majority of students and university graduates are women. in the eu, only one in ten board members of companies is a woman and only 3% of ceos are female. the gender pay gap remains at an average of 18% in the eu. if europe is to achieve the objectives of sustainable growth, employment, competitiveness and social cohesion, it will have to continue to combat the still existing inequalities between men and women, which is why i supported this report.
in writing. - i voted against this because, although i agree with many of the points adopted, there are aspects which, in my view, should be deleted. working conditions and access to employment for women have become more difficult in the wake of the crisis we are living in. i therefore agree with the subject dealt with in the european commission report on the need to mainstream gender equality in all policies and in the early education of european children. the fight against violence against women must also continue through awareness campaigns and school education. i do not agree, however, with quotas in the private sector, lists of vulnerable women and the guarantee of a minimum wage, which i consider impossible to implement.
in writing. - on 8 march, international women's day, i would like to congratulate ms mariya nedelcheva on her report on equality between men and women. i share your analysis that women have been particularly affected by the economic and financial crisis we are going through. all indications are that in employment, health, education, social support and other sectors, women will feel the consequences of the crisis more strongly and for longer than men. in terms of income levels, working and recruitment conditions and access to work, the situation of women appears to be deteriorating more rapidly than that of men. in this regard, it is important to create new opportunities and strengthen gender equality synergies, helping to stimulate recovery and economic growth itself. i welcome the reference to the fight against poverty (as 2010 was the european year for the eradication of poverty), with particular attention to the most vulnerable women. i regret that the parliamentary left has also introduced the abortion controversy here, without taking account of the community's powers.
in writing. as i have said before in this house, 'men and women must be treated equally, given the same rights but with special consideration for their needs, which in the case of women is particularly evident in areas such as maternity protection and the reconciliation of work and family life ...'. i am therefore pleased to note that among other things there is concern about the protection of mothers and the support of the elderly at home, which are often the responsibility of women within the family, making it difficult for them to enter the workforce. but unlike the rapporteur, whose views are very clear, i do not agree that gender equality is achieved through quota systems. quotas are the undermining of women, who are promoted to certain positions solely on the basis of their gender and not on the basis of their competence, ability or appetite. the commission's intention to apply them to private undertakings is therefore inadmissible. finally, as a staunch supporter of the principle of subsidiarity, i believe that many of the issues discussed in this report, although important and relevant, should remain within the sphere of the autonomy of the states. that is also why i did not vote in favour.

in writing. - despite efforts to achieve equality between men and women, women are still at a higher risk of poverty (17%) than men (15%), with the difference being greater for older people (22% of women versus 17% of men). the higher risk of poverty affecting women is partly due to the existing gender pay gap. this wage gap remains at an average of 18% in the european union, with repercussions on lifetime earnings, social protection and pensions. this report, which has won my support, calls on the member states to take gender equality into account in their recovery plans from the recession, to do so by promoting and increasing the employment of women, the inclusion of flexible working hours in the labour market, equal pay and the revision of tax and retirement pension systems.

madam president, i come from a country which has existed for eight centuries and which is nevertheless interested in having, in this globalised world, a strong europe and a europe which is able to dialogue face to face with china, india and the united states. the crisis we are experiencing is not a crisis in the euro zone, it is, as someone said, a crisis in the euro zone and it is a crisis in the euro zone because a single currency can only work when there is a serious and persistent work of convergence between the different areas that make it up in terms of growth rates, the level of income, employment, when there is real convergence and we have been working so far on nominal convergence indicators, which is not at all the same thing. in this sense, it is urgent that europe should complete what it has started, and in order to complete what it has started, in particular the single currency, it must in fact create a solid stability fund, a fund which will enable countries in difficulty to achieve this convergence with acceptable and non-prohibitive interest rates and which will not have to cut back on the strategic investment which allows them to achieve this convergence and which will enable them to pay back with this growth what they borrowed in the crisis. mr president, we need an active committee, a committee which is involved in the construction of this stability fund, but also in the eurobonds, and which hears the message which parliament has left it today through the new source of own resources, which must be an effective reinforcement of a budget which is manifestly insufficient. we have just adopted the podimata report which clearly advocates a financial transaction tax. europe must change course at this moment of change if it is to survive, it needs a strong parliament, but also a commission capable not only of reacting but of acting, taking the initiatives we are anxiously awaiting so that this experience is not lost, so that this experience bears fruit.

president of the commission. - madam president, there were some specific questions about portugal, and i will answer them. whether portugal should use the financial stability fund or not is a decision of the portuguese authorities. it is precisely because it concerns the sovereign debt that it is a sovereign decision of portugal. what i can tell you, of course, is that the financial stability fund and the use of that fund, as well as the imf's aid, was designed as a last resort, ultima ratio. it is obvious that if a country can avoid using this mechanism it should avoid it, there are costs to using these bailout funds, not just reputational costs. so if a country can avoid it, it should avoid it, but again, it is a decision of the national authorities whether or not to use this rescue fund, or at least to apply to activate this fund. secondly, what i would like to see in this fund is not a matter of taste, it is a matter of policy, and we in the commission are actively working with the states, particularly the eurozone states, to strengthen this fund in its lending capacity and also to broaden the scope of its activities, including greater flexibility. some of these issues are extremely sensitive from the point of view of the markets, which is why i do not think it is prudent to announce intentions that are not being realised, but it is a work in progress within the euro area. and as you know, the commission, particularly in its annual growth assessment, has clearly put forward the proposal for strengthening the fund and extending its activities. if this policy should or can be changed, i can tell you right now that, in relation to the most vulnerable countries, it cannot be changed. it would be totally irresponsible for countries with such a high level of public or private debt to slow down their efforts at this time to consolidate their budgets and to carry out structural reforms. when a country has such a high level of debt it must regain the confidence of the markets, otherwise its economic situation becomes unsustainable. so if we want to help the countries which are currently in the most vulnerable situation, we must not come up with mirages, with something that is unrealistic, but we must, on the contrary, support the serious efforts they can make towards fiscal consolidation and structural reforms. only then can they have the confidence of the markets. of course, it is not just the effort of the individual country that needs a joint effort of the euro area. this is what is being developed with, of course, differentiated commitment between the different actors. what i can tell you is that the commission has done everything, everything in its power, to propose more ambition. but as you know, the commission proposes that in the end, particularly in matters which are strictly national competence, such as matters which were not provided for in the treaty, as is the case with the financial stability fund, the decision is taken by the member states, in particular the euro zone states. in any case, what i would like to say to the whole parliament is that many of the criticisms i have heard here today - even if most of them support the general line proposed by the commission - are addressed, if i understand correctly, to certain governments or to certain member states. so, it's not for me to speak on their behalf. what i have to say is that the commission has presented a package of proposals for governance. we have tested the ambition of our governments to the limit. even for the governance package presented by myself and my colleague olli rehn, the member states did not want to accept the initial level of ambition. it is true that we have submitted legislative proposals. now, what has emerged is a new idea, like that of the competitiveness pact which we are trying to put as much as possible into the community method. i have made clear to you the efforts the commission is making to ensure that this idea of the impact of competitiveness can be useful, can have added value, either for growth and employment, which, as i said, clearly remains the priority for the commission, or even to strengthen the governance system. of course, the commission does not need to be reminded of its role as guarantor of the treaty. we have shown this without fail, whether it be on the questions of the internal market, competition or non-discrimination. i can assure you once again that the commission would not hesitate to resort to any means if we thought that principles or rules of the treaty would be called into question by the decisions of either the european council or any other institution. that is why our work is a long-term, of course, serious work that we do with a sense of responsibility. it is obvious that we are in an extremely delicate moment, you know, a moment where the first thing that many governments try to see in the morning is the evolution of the spreads of their public debts. so what we say is not indifferent. the hopes we have are not indifferent. the commission must therefore be ambitious and at the same time responsible for making proposals even though they have a chance of being carried out, rather than simply an effect of announcement followed by an effect of deception. that is what i want to avoid, that is what the commission must avoid. so it is an effect of deception, or an effect of pure division, whether within the euro zone or even within the union as a whole. that is why i can assure you that the commission will remain with the greatest ambition. it is the commission which is now telling all the governments that parliament must be associated with this competitiveness pact. it is the commission that is telling governments that it must retain a central role in this competitiveness pact, not because of an institutional fetish, not because of any ego of the institution, but because i believe that the commission and the community method are the guarantee of avoiding the division between the euro zone and the rest of europe. this is the guarantee of avoiding attacks on the integrity of the single market; it is the guarantee of avoiding the jeopardization of other mechanisms such as the stability and growth pact: it is the guarantee, of course, that we will remain european within the framework of the european union with european solidarity. so i was extremely frank, extremely open. in all transparency, the commission does its work, constructively of course, in trying to save an idea which, if it is well presented and done in a community approach, could bring added value to our governance efforts, not as some of you have pointed out. the commission has always been guided by the governments' efforts to coordinate economic policy, and so have most of the members of this parliament. we therefore have a chance. and if the heads of state and government wish to continue to invest themselves in this coordination of economic policies, and included in some areas which are hitherto considered to be only of national competence, i think we should welcome it insofar as it adds value to growth and employment, insofar as it respects the systems of community governance. that is what is at issue here. i think the debate has been very useful from this point of view. i believe that the message from this parliament has reached the european council. president buzek sent it the last time he was in the european council. i believe that, in the main, the commission and parliament will be firm in defence of the community approach, being sure that this is the only way for europe to achieve the objectives which are ours for the euro area, for stability but also for growth and employment in the union as a whole.

madam president, commissioner, i should like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr langen, and the shadow rapporteurs, in particular mrs grossetête, for the good work they have done. europe is currently facing a decline in its competitiveness in global markets. in this sense, europe must find ways to strengthen its industrial base to meet the new challenges. this report presents proposals to revive european industry. an integrated and sustainable industrial policy should be based on scientific research, innovation, increased resource efficiency, a strategy for raw materials, the efforts of smes and the development of regional networks. in particular, it is essential that energy efficiency and the introduction of information and communication technologies in industrial sectors form the basis of this new industrial revolution in order to increase competitiveness, economic growth and employment. i particularly welcome the emphasis the report places on traditional european industry, which is fundamental to our economy. measures such as the introduction of new technologies and a further strengthening of scientific research and innovation in sectors such as manufacturing are of crucial importance. only then will it be possible to put european industry back in the world leadership position so necessary for jobs and economic growth in europe.
this discussion of the difficulties in accessing raw materials such as rare earths is inseparable from the current state of the world economy and the systemic crisis in which we find ourselves. the crisis that we have been told is financial is in fact a wider and more global crisis. it is a crisis that also lies in the confrontation between economic growth as understood by capitalism and a planet earth that is generous but that is finite. it is also in this inability to understand nature and its limits that lie the causes of a system, capitalism, that subordinates everything to the dynamics of profit and accumulation, but nature does indeed have its limits. the evolution towards a polycentric world, both economically and politically, opens the way to the rise of competition for resources, which provokes and feeds conflicts. the currency and trade wars we have seen are troubling symptoms, but they are not isolated. other wars are emerging as threats for the present and the future, and these are also the issues that are discussed when we discuss what brought us here today.
fossil fuels now provide the vast majority of primary energy needs worldwide. over 80% of the total, oil 34%, coal 26% and natural gas 21%. these resources have, as we know, been exploited at rates far in excess of their natural replacement rates, with their inexorable depletion looming on the horizon. the situation of natural gas is comparable to that of oil, except that its distribution is more limited and its transport and storage are more difficult. the commission has already made a number of proposals. there are no silver bullets and the remaining fossil fuel reserves must be managed very carefully, with wisdom and thrift. but whatever alternatives are found for energy provision, it is almost certain that overall energy consumption will have to decline from present levels and there is not necessarily much harm in that. we must prepare ourselves for this scenario.
the libyan uprising cannot be understood without the revolutions in tunisia and egypt. it is precisely because this uprising in libya is part of a historic, revolutionary and popular process that will bring democracy to the southern mediterranean and the entire arab world, that the position and the change in the european position in relation to the way it has acted in libya is so important. the days of the gaddafi regime are numbered because it is a dictatorship and the people have lost their fear. because it cannot survive with neighbours in democratic transition and also because it is isolated in the international community. but this change in the european position is bound to say something about the past. because the european union was one of the pillars of the old regime. the resolution does not say so, but the weapons with which the libyan people are being repressed are largely european weapons and bombs. so i want to be very clear. the left is in favour of freezing assets, it is in favour of an arms embargo, it is in favour of dealing with the insurgency, it is in favour of all humanitarian aid measures, but i also want to make it clear that we are against any military intervention, including the measure that may open the doors to them, the no-fly zone. we have spoken about lucidity. we have the experience, we know how military measures start and we know how they never end once they start.
mr president, the european parliament seconds the united nations in their unanimous message to the libyan dictator: step down, stop the bloodshed, face justice. in the face of gaddafi’s retaliation against his people, the eu must exercise the responsibility to protect by helping to enforce a no-fly zone, as envisaged by the arab league, the oic and the african union, and the other measures decided on by the security council, with all means available, including csdp assets – please note, mrs ashton – namely, to enforce the arms embargo. the eu must do more to assist all those trying to escape or who are stranded in libya by supporting unhcr and humanitarian organisations on the ground and by helping to resettle refugees who cannot be repatriated, such as somalis, eritreans and ethiopians. a burden-sharing action plan to resettle refugees, a common asylum system, temporary protection measures – all should urgently be enacted by the european union in compliance with the solidarity clause and the principle of non-refoulement, and as part of a coherent and long-term strategy to deal with the impact of political transition in the north of africa, addressing the root causes of migration. the eu must revise the enp south, must prioritise support for capacity and institution-building to sustain the rule of law, human rights, including women’s rights, and to prepare genuine elections. the eu must immediately establish relations with emerging political forces in libya, namely the interim transitional council, to encourage democratic transition and to ensure that democracy delivers the freedoms, the development and the dignity that the libyan people are showing us they aspire to.

author. − mr president, commissioner, it has been two years since the commission launched a communication in february 2009 on a community approach to the prevention of natural and man-made disasters. the importance of this issue is overwhelming. since then, several disasters have struck europe with profound negative consequences for the people, the territory, the economy and the environment. the commission's communication has generally followed a correct approach, but it is not sufficient, as this parliament has come to believe. the commission is also slow to implement the commitments it has itself made in that communication. for example, the commitment to draw up a catalogue of prevention measures to be financed by the european union and implemented by the member states. two years later, where is this catalogue? will the commission wait for the next multiannual financial framework to present it? two more years? however, in september last year this parliament adopted a report on the same subject. a report which comes forward with a set of important recommendations. it is important to say that this report was preceded by a very wide-ranging debate, not only here in parliament but also with a wide range of national, regional and local bodies involved in the various phases of the disaster management cycle. the report also draws on the experience of the people affected by disasters over the past year. let me mention here some of the specific points of the report among the many that it contains. a series of measures has been defined to provide priority support to member states for the correction of risk-inducing situations in areas such as forestry management, protection and defence of the coastline, the restoration and protection of watersheds, the protection and rehabilitation of inhabited areas particularly vulnerable to certain types of disasters, and the maintenance of agricultural activity in areas affected by depopulation and at risk of natural disasters. how has the commission included, or intends to include, these areas in the catalogue of measures which it has yet to draw up? the report also proposed the creation of a european public agricultural insurance scheme and the establishment of a system of minimum compensation for farmers affected by disasters. i would point out that this is very different from the possibility that currently exists with the cap health check of member states subsidising insurance internally. what is being proposed is an insurance funded by community funds which will put all farmers on an equal footing in terms of protection against disasters, whether farmers in the member states with the greatest difficulties or farmers in rich countries. disasters are, as we know, deeply unjust, almost always affecting those who have the least means of protecting themselves, whether they are individuals or states. if there is one area where the solidarity of the european union and the principle of cohesion should have visible expression, it is in the protection of people, the economy and the environment in the face of disasters. so i ask what the commission has done or will do to reduce the disparities between regions and member states in this area. in particular, by helping to improve prevention in regions and member states with a high risk exposure and lower economic capacity. another area covered in the report is the strengthening of early warning systems in the member states and the establishment of links between the various early warning systems. what steps have been taken in this regard? what are the next steps? finally, it should be remembered that, in the context of prevention and in the light of the experience gained in recent disasters, it is imperative to revise the solidarity fund regulation to allow for a more flexible and timely mobilisation of this instrument. what has the commission done, or what is it going to do, for this review? i would remind you that a year ago the island of madeira was struck by a major disaster, one which caused deaths and considerable material damage to strategic infrastructure and essential equipment. a year later, not a penny of european union aid reached madeira. what will the commission do to change this situation when the solidarity fund regulation currently says that it must make it possible to contribute to the rapid restoration of normal living conditions, it must act swiftly and effectively and contribute quickly to the mobilization of relief resources? where's the speed when a year later not a penny has reached madeira island? in conclusion, mr president, i would once again urge the commission to take the broad consensus that this report has gathered during its discussion and vote as a clear sign that these recommendations, the recommendations in the report, are to be put into practice. many of these recommendations were already contained in previous resolutions of this parliament and unfortunately nothing has been done and the commission has particular responsibilities in this area.
member of the commission. − mr president, i wish to thank parliament for the opportunity to exchange views on disaster prevention, and mr ferreira in particular for his continued interest in the subject. the disasters of last year were a salutary reminder that the eu and its member states need to step up work on disaster prevention. we need to be ambitious. we all know that investing in disaster prevention pays off. at the same time, ensuring cost-effective and increased investment in disaster prevention is a challenge. we are now assessing the effectiveness of existing eu financing instruments. we are also developing a catalogue of prevention measures that would be considered by member states for eu funding. our objective is to increase the impact of eu funding and to accelerate the implementation of regional fund support. we are also looking at innovative financing instruments, such as insurance pooling to share risks. effective investments in disaster prevention will help to save lives, limit damages and, ultimately, save money. actions are also under way to improve our knowledge of disasters. we have worked with the european environment agency on a report assessing the frequency of disasters in europe and their impact on humans, the economies and ecosystems. we also need clear and transparent assessments of the risks we face. on 21 december last year we issued a guidance paper on national risk assessment and mapping to encourage member states in fostering a comprehensive risk-management culture. developing fully-fledged risk management policies will require the involvement of all actors. the increased frequency and intensity of disasters in europe should also provide further incentives for member states to invest in preparedness and build up their capacity. besides the prevention elements, it is equally important that member states, and europe as a whole, are able to provide the best possible response. in october last year we outlined our policy proposal for a european disaster-response capacity. our objective is to improve the efficiency, the coherence and the visibility of the eu’s response to disasters.
i am not saying that we should not be concerned about the future of the european union. sadly, natural and man-made disasters are becoming more frequent and more devastating. although the responsibility for disaster prevention lies primarily with the member states, the european union can make an important contribution. there are already some community instruments to support these disaster prevention activities. but it is important that these instruments are assessed so that we can better identify the gaps. in addition, there is also a need to improve the financing mechanisms. it has already been mentioned here and i repeat what happened to madeira, that there has been no response yet to the promised support and it is clear that the victims of this catastrophe cannot wait indefinitely. the commission has also been asked on several occasions to develop community guidelines for risk mapping. i would also like to stress the importance of a complete inventory of sources of information, because only with reliable information is it possible to act appropriately. some of the suggestions and proposals in the ferreira report were already in my report which was approved by parliament in 2006, and the commission has not yet responded to many of these proposals. i would therefore like to ask the commissioner if he can tell us about the work done so far to set up the european drought observatory and also in relation to the directive on forest fires.
for the gue/ngl group i would like to begin by saying that i fully support what my colleague has said. the prevention of natural and man-made disasters is of enormous and growing importance and the european commission systematically presents us with a number of procedural and timetable intentions. but there is a very complicated problem, as has already been mentioned. the solidarity fund is the instrument that normally responds to these situations, but it responds in a very, very long time, from nine months to a year, and that after the disaster. as has already been said, and i will repeat it again and repeat it again as often as necessary, there is the case of madeira, which suffered a major catastrophe a year ago and has not yet received any support. and so i ask, and i reinforce this question: is it not time for the commission to review the procedure for the fund itself and the financing model itself? how can we maintain an emergency fund to deal with situations that are increasingly chronic? we don't know where it's going to happen, but we know it's going to happen, and climate change is there to prove it. therefore, the exception can never respond to a situation of regularity.
mr president, the concerns raised here in the field of disaster prevention and response are a matter of great sensitivity and of the utmost importance to our populations which should not and cannot be delayed. we are talking about very sensitive situations affecting the safety of people and their property, which often move us all by the loss of lives, by the destruction of families, by the destruction of entire working lives. but all our demonstrations in the face of tragedies, which in a media way impress everyone and make everyone aware, are worthless if we then fall asleep to the work we must do so that those situations can be avoided, minimized or better assisted. commissioner, my colleagues have focused the matter very well here. it is a matter where the european union can best demonstrate its presence with its citizens, helping them to prevent disasters and, above all, when they occur, to be at their side when they are most in need and most vulnerable.

in writing. as i said when i spoke in the debate on the priorities of the hungarian presidency, these are matters of hungary's internal life which can be, and have been, regulated in a healthy and normal relationship between the european commission and the hungarian government and parliament. as a defender of freedoms, in particular freedom of expression and of the press, i can only congratulate myself on the results achieved.
